sourceWitness.quote: 帝報曰：「見汝二十字，諸兒作中，最為優者。

context.zh: 少時又無棋局，乃破荻為片，縱橫以為棋局，指點行勢，遂至名品。

translations.literal: In youth he also had no chess board, so he broke reeds into strips and laid them crosswise as a board, pointing out moves and positions, until he reached master rank.
translations.idiomatic: As a boy he had no chessboard either, so he split reeds into strips and laid them crosswise to make one, calling out moves and positions until he reached master rank.

context.zh: 性剛穎俊出，與諸王共作短句詩，學謝靈運體，以呈高帝。

translations.literal: His nature was firm, sharp, and outstanding; with the other princes he composed short-verse poems in Xie Lingyun's style and presented them to Emperor Gao.
translations.idiomatic: His temperament was bold, sharp, and outstanding; with the other princes he wrote short poems in the manner of Xie Lingyun and presented them to Emperor Gao.

context.zh: 帝報曰：「見汝二十字，諸兒作中，最為優者。

translations.literal: The emperor replied: "Seeing your twenty characters—among all the boys' compositions yours is the finest.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor replied: "I have seen your twenty lines—among all my sons' compositions, yours is the finest.

context.zh: 但康樂放蕩，作體不辨有首尾，安仁、士衡深可宗尚，顏延之抑其次也。」

translations.literal: But Xie Kangyue is unrestrained; his compositional form does not distinguish beginning from end. Pan Anren and Lu Shiheng are deeply worthy of reverence; Yan Yanzhi ranks below them."
translations.idiomatic: But Kangyue is unrestrained—his compositions lack clear structure from beginning to end. Anren and Shiheng are truly worthy of emulation; Yanzhi ranks below them."

context.zh: 建元二年，為會稽太守，加都督。

proposals.before: Jin General Who Pacifies the North Wei Guan made Cao a gate officer; he was repeatedly sent to the state and rather attached himself on his own.
proposals.after: Jin General Who Campaigns in the North Wei Guan made Cao a gate officer; he was repeatedly sent to the state and rather attached himself on his own.
proposals.reason: 征北 means campaigning north, distinct from 鎮北 pacifying/guarding north. Preserve the actual appointment and named actors.

sourceWitness.quote: 晉征北將軍衞瓘以操為牙門將，數使於國，頗自結附。

context.zh: 衞操，字德元，代人也。

translations.literal: Wei Cao, styled Deyuan, was a man of Dai.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Cao, whose style was Deyuan, came from Dai.

context.zh: 少通俠，有才略。

translations.literal: In youth he mastered chivalry and possessed talent and stratagem.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man he lived by the code of the knight-errant and showed both talent and strategic mind.

context.zh: 晉征北將軍衞瓘以操為牙門將，數使於國，頗自結附。

translations.literal: Jin General Who Pacifies the North Wei Guan made Cao a gate officer; he was repeatedly sent to the state and rather attached himself on his own.
translations.idiomatic: Jin's General Who Pacifies the North, Wei Guan, appointed Cao gate officer and often sent him on missions to the Dai state, where Cao gradually built ties of his own.

context.zh: 始祖崩後，與從子雄及其宗室鄉親姬澹等十數人，同來歸國，說桓穆二帝招納晉人，於是晉人附者稍眾。

translations.literal: After the founding ancestor died, together with his nephew Xiong and more than ten clansmen and fellow-townsmen such as Ji Dan, he came in a body to return to the state, urging the Huan and Mu emperors to recruit Jin people; thereafter those of Jin who attached themselves grew somewhat numerous.
translations.idiomatic: When the founding ancestor passed away, Cao came home with his nephew Xiong and a dozen-odd kinsmen and neighbors, among them Ji Dan, and urged the Huan and Mu emperors to welcome Jin subjects. From then on Jin adherents grew steadily in number.

context.zh: 桓帝嘉之，以為輔相，任以國事。

translations.literal: Emperor Huan commended this and made him chief minister, entrusting him with state affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huan approved and named him chief minister, charging him with the affairs of the realm.

rejectedWorkerOverliteralRepairs.reason: An established person may be identified by full name in idiomatic English; South Wind is not a necessary improvement over Jia Nanfeng. Correct unsupported explicit Chinese name-attestation claims separately.
Prior s0044 explicitly identifies Xie Lingyun; established courtesy-name identifications may be expanded. The actual error is Kangle’s reading, not the presence of explanatory surnames.

Absence of expanded given names from this abbreviated literary allusion alone does not prove a mistranslation. Preserve the English pending specific evidence that an identification is wrong; do not strip helpful identifiers merely for literalness.
